results.title: Shi's question on element-order counts (Kourovka 18.112)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proposition that if a finite group $G$ has the property that, for every divisor $d > 1$ of $|G|$ and every subgroup $H$ of $G$ whose order is coprime to $d$, $|H|$ divides the number of elements of $G$ of order $d$, then every non-identity element of $G$ has prime-power order.

results.title: Counting elements of each order forces prime-power orders
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group such that for every divisor $d > 1$ of $|G|$ and every subgroup $H$ of $G$ whose order is coprime to $d$, the order $|H|$ divides the number of elements of $G$ of order $d$. Then every non-identity element of $G$ has prime-power order.

results.title: Algebra maps from a DVR into a finite local DVR extension are local
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be discrete valuation rings, with $B$ and $C$ algebras over $A$, where $C$ is finite as an $A$-module and the structure map $A \to C$ is a local homomorphism. Then every $A$-algebra homomorphism $B \to C$ is a local homomorphism.

results.title: Induced map on residue fields of DVR extensions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be discrete valuation rings, with $B$ and $C$ algebras over $A$ whose structure maps are local homomorphisms, where $C$ is finite as an $A$-module. Write $\kappa(R)$ for the residue field of a local ring $R$. An $A$-algebra homomorphism $f \colon B \to C$ induces the $\kappa(A)$-algebra homomorphism $\kappa(B) \to \kappa(C)$ that sends the residue class of $b \in B$ to the residue class of $f(b)$.

results.title: Residue-field maps determine algebra maps out of a formally unramified DVR extension
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be discrete valuation rings, with $B$ and $C$ algebras over $A$ whose structure maps are local homomorphisms, where $C$ is finite as an $A$-module and $B$ is formally unramified over $A$. Write $\kappa(R)$ for the residue field of a local ring $R$. Then two $A$-algebra homomorphisms $B \to C$ that induce the same $\kappa(A)$-algebra homomorphism $\kappa(B) \to \kappa(C)$ are equal.

results.title: Lucas parameters of the k-Jacobsthal numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $k$, the Lucas-sequence parameters $(P, Q) = (k, -2)$. The Lucas sequences $J_{k,n} = U_n(k, -2)$ and $j_{k,n} = V_n(k, -2)$ with these parameters are the $k$-Jacobsthal numbers ($J_{k,0} = 0$, $J_{k,1} = 1$) and the $k$-Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers ($j_{k,0} = 2$, $j_{k,1} = k$); both satisfy $x_{n+2} = k x_{n+1} + 2 x_n$.

results.title: The second k-Jacobsthal number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$, the $k$-Jacobsthal number $J_{k,2} = U_2(k, -2)$ equals $k$.

results.title: The $k$-Jacobsthal-Lucas number $j_{k,2}$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$, the $k$-Jacobsthal-Lucas numbers $j_{k,n} = V_n(k, -2)$, the Lucas sequence $V$ with parameters $(P, Q) = (k, -2)$, satisfy $j_{k,2} = k^2 + 4$.

results.title: Companion $k$-Jacobsthal numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $k$ and integers $a, b$, the companion $k$-Jacobsthal numbers $\mathcal{J}_{k,n}(a, b)$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, are the integers defined by $\mathcal{J}_{k,0}(a, b) = a$, $\mathcal{J}_{k,1}(a, b) = b$ and $\mathcal{J}_{k,n+2}(a, b) = k\,\mathcal{J}_{k,n+1}(a, b) + 2\,\mathcal{J}_{k,n}(a, b)$.

results.title: Recurrence of the companion $k$-Jacobsthal numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$, all integers $a, b$ and every natural number $n$, the companion $k$-Jacobsthal numbers satisfy $\mathcal{J}_{k,n+2}(a, b) = k\,\mathcal{J}_{k,n+1}(a, b) + 2\,\mathcal{J}_{k,n}(a, b)$.

results.title: The second companion $k$-Jacobsthal number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$ and all integers $a, b$, the companion $k$-Jacobsthal numbers satisfy $\mathcal{J}_{k,2}(a, b) = bk + 2a$.

results.title: The $k$-Jacobsthal numbers as companion numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $k$, let $\mathcal{J}_{k,n}(a, b)$ denote the companion $k$-Jacobsthal numbers and $J_{k,n} = U_n(k, -2)$ the $k$-Jacobsthal numbers, the Lucas sequence with parameters $(k, -2)$. Then for every natural number $n$, $\mathcal{J}_{k,n}(0, 1) = J_{k,n}$: the companion numbers with initial values $0$ and $1$ are the $k$-Jacobsthal numbers.

results.title: Binet-type identities for k-Jacobsthal numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let $J_{k,n} = U_n(k, -2)$ and $j_{k,n} = V_n(k, -2)$ be the $k$-Jacobsthal and $k$-Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers, and let $\Delta_k = \sqrt{k^2 + 8}$ and $\sigma_k = (k + \Delta_k)/2$. Then, in $\mathbb{R}$, $j_{k,n} + \Delta_k J_{k,n} = 2\sigma_k^n$ and $j_{k,n} - \Delta_k J_{k,n} = 2(-2)^n / \sigma_k^n$, and, in $\mathbb{Z}$, $j_{k,n}^2 - (k^2 + 8) J_{k,n}^2 = (-2)^{n+2}$.

results.title: Addition formulas for k-Jacobsthal numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k$, $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers and let $J_{k,n} = U_n(k, -2)$ and $j_{k,n} = V_n(k, -2)$ be the $k$-Jacobsthal and $k$-Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers. Then $2J_{k,m+n} = J_{k,m} j_{k,n} + J_{k,n} j_{k,m}$ and $2j_{k,m+n} = j_{k,m} j_{k,n} + (k^2 + 8) J_{k,m} J_{k,n}$.

results.title: Summand of Ramanujan's general theta function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For complex numbers $a$, $b$ and an integer $n$, this is the term $a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$ of index $n$ in Ramanujan's general theta function $f(a,b) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{k(k+1)/2} b^{k(k-1)/2}$.

results.title: Raw Ramanujan theta sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For complex numbers $a$ and $b$, the raw Ramanujan theta sum is $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$ when this series is summable, and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Ramanujan's general theta function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For complex numbers $a$ and $b$ such that the series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$ is summable, Ramanujan's general theta function is its sum $f(a,b) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$.

results.title: Ramanujan's theta series diverges at $a = b = 1$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$ of Ramanujan's general theta function is not summable at $a = b = 1$, since every one of its terms equals $1$.

results.title: The raw Ramanujan theta sum vanishes at $a = b = 1$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The raw Ramanujan theta sum $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$, which is assigned the value $0$ whenever the series is not summable, equals $0$ at $a = b = 1$, because there every term equals $1$ and the series is not summable.

results.title: Busy Beaver machine
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A Busy Beaver machine with $n$ working states is a transition table that assigns to each of the $n$ working states and each read symbol in $\{0, 1\}$ a symbol in $\{0, 1\}$ to write, a head movement (left or right), and a next state, which is either one of the $n$ working states or the halt state.

results.title: Busy Beaver machine configuration
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A configuration of an $n$-state machine consists of a current state, which is either one of the $n$ working states or the halt state, an integer head position, and a tape assigning a symbol in $\{0, 1\}$ to every integer cell.

results.summary: Let $M$ be a machine with $n$ working states and let $c$ be a configuration with head position $h$. If $c$ is halted, the step leaves $c$ unchanged. Otherwise let $q$ be the current state, let $a$ be the symbol in cell $h$, and let $M(q, a) = (b, d, q')$. The step writes $b$ in cell $h$, leaving every other cell unchanged, moves the head to $h - 1$ if $d$ is left and to $h + 1$ if $d$ is right, and passes to the…

results.title: Initial state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a machine with $n$ working states, the initial state is state $0$ when $n > 0$, and the halt state when $n = 0$.

results.title: Initial configuration of a Busy Beaver machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The initial configuration of a machine with $n$ working states is in the initial state (state $0$, or the halt state when $n = 0$), with the head at position $0$ and every tape cell blank, that is, holding the symbol $0$.

results.title: Configuration after $t$ steps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Busy Beaver machine $M$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the configuration of $M$ after $t$ steps is the result of applying the one-step map of $M$ $t$ times to the initial configuration on the blank tape.

results.title: Halting within $t$ steps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A Busy Beaver machine $M$ with $n$ working states halts within $t$ steps when the configuration reached after running $M$ for $t$ steps from the initial blank-tape configuration is in the halt state.

results.title: Halting on the blank tape
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A Busy Beaver machine $M$ halts when there is a number of steps $t$ such that $M$ halts within $t$ steps, that is, when $M$ started from the initial blank-tape configuration eventually reaches the halt state.

results.title: Halting time
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an $n$-state machine $M$ that halts on the blank tape, its halting time is the least $t$ such that $M$, started on the blank tape, is in the halt state after $t$ steps.

results.title: Head displacement bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$-state Busy Beaver machine $M$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, if $h \in \mathbb{Z}$ is the head position after $M$ has run for $t$ steps from the initial configuration on the blank tape, then $|h| \le t$.

results.title: Cells far from the origin stay blank
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a machine with $n$ working states, started in cell $0$ on the blank tape. For every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ and every cell $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|i| > t$, the symbol in cell $i$ after $t$ steps is $0$.

results.title: Number of ones after $t$ steps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Busy Beaver machine $M$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps is the number of cells $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $-t \le i \le t$ that hold the symbol $1$ in the configuration of $M$ after $t$ steps, started on the blank tape.

results.title: After $t$ steps, every one lies within distance $t$ of the origin
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Busy Beaver machine $M$, every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ and every cell $i \in \mathbb{Z}$, if cell $i$ holds the symbol $1$ after $M$ runs for $t$ steps from the initial blank-tape configuration, then $-t \le i \le t$.

results.title: The number of ones grows by at most one per step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Busy Beaver machine $M$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of ones of $M$ after $t + 1$ steps is at most the number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps plus $1$.

results.title: At most $t$ ones after $t$ steps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Busy Beaver machine $M$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps is at most $t$.

results.title: Runtime of a Busy Beaver machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a machine $M$ with $n$ working states, the runtime of $M$ is its halting time on the blank tape if $M$ halts, and $0$ if $M$ does not halt. This is the quantity whose maximum over all $n$-state machines is the shift function $S(n)$.

results.title: Score of a machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Busy Beaver machine $M$: if $M$ halts on the blank tape, with halting time $T$, its score is the number of ones of $M$ after $T$ steps; if $M$ does not halt, its score is $0$.

results.title: Busy Beaver shift function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, Rado's shift function $S(n)$ is the largest halting time of an $n$-state two-symbol machine that halts when started on the blank tape; machines that do not halt contribute $0$.

results.title: Busy Beaver score function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, Rado's score function $\Sigma(n)$ is the largest number of ones left on the tape, at its halting time, by an $n$-state two-symbol machine that halts when started on the blank tape; machines that do not halt contribute $0$.

results.title: The Busy Beaver score is at most the shift
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, Rado's score function $\Sigma$ and Rado's shift function $S$ satisfy $\Sigma(n) \le S(n)$: the largest number of ones left on the tape by a halting $n$-state two-symbol machine started on the blank tape is at most the largest halting time of such a machine.

results.title: The shift function is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S(n)$ be Rado's shift function, the largest runtime of an $n$-state machine, where the runtime of a machine is its halting time on the blank tape if it halts and $0$ otherwise. For every $n$, some $n$-state machine $M$ has runtime equal to $S(n)$. Thus $S(n)$ is the halting time of a halting $n$-state machine, or $S(n) = 0$.

results.title: The score function is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Sigma(n)$ be the busy beaver score function, the largest score of an $n$-state machine, where the score of a machine is the number of ones on its final tape if it halts on the blank tape and $0$ otherwise. For every $n$, some $n$-state machine $M$ has score equal to $\Sigma(n)$. Thus $\Sigma(n)$ is the number of ones left by a halting $n$-state machine, or $\Sigma(n) = 0$.

results.title: Embedding a machine into one more state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An $n$-state machine $M$ is embedded into $n + 1$ states as follows. In a working state $q < n$ reading a symbol $s$, the new machine writes the symbol, makes the move and enters the next state that $M$ prescribes in state $q$ on $s$, halting when $M$ halts. In the new state $n$ it writes $0$, moves left and halts, whatever it reads.

results.title: Embedding a configuration into one more state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a configuration $c$ of an $n$-state machine, its embedding is the configuration for $n + 1$ states with the same head position and the same tape as $c$. Its state is the state of $c$, where a working state $q \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ stays $q$ and the halt state stays the halt state.

results.title: A one-state machine that stays in its state on a blank never halts
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Busy Beaver machine with a single working state $0$. If the transition of $M$ from state $0$ on reading the blank symbol $0$ has next state $0$, then $M$ does not halt.

results.title: One-state machines halt within one step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every halting one-state machine halts within one step.

results.title: Machine code
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The code of a machine $M$ with $n$ working states is the natural number that encodes the pair $(n, i)$ under a fixed pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, where $i$ is the index of $M$ in a fixed enumeration of the finitely many machines with $n$ working states.

results.title: Sentence codes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The sentence code with tag $a$ and payload $p$ is the natural number $4p + a$. The tags in use are $0$ (the coded machine halts), $1$ (the coded machine does not halt), $2$ (the false sentence), and $3$ with payload the pairing code of $n$ and $B$ (every halting $n$-state machine halts within $B$ steps).

results.title: Halting sentence of a machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an $n$-state machine $M$, the halting sentence of $M$ is the sentence code with tag $0$ and payload the code of $M$. It stands for "$M$ halts on the blank tape"; this meaning comes from soundness hypotheses on a theory, not from the code itself.

results.title: Non-halting sentence of a machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Busy Beaver machine $M$, the non-halting sentence of $M$ is the sentence code with tag $1$ whose payload is the code of $M$; it stands for "$M$ does not halt on the blank tape".

results.title: The false sentence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The false sentence is the sentence code with tag $2$ and payload $0$, that is, the natural number $2$.

results.title: Runtime-bound sentence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $B$, the runtime-bound sentence is the sentence code with tag $3$ and payload $\langle n, B \rangle$, the pairing of $n$ and $B$; as a number it equals $4 \langle n, B \rangle + 3$.

results.title: Formal theory
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A formal theory is given by a provability predicate on sentence codes, which are natural numbers: for each natural number it specifies whether that sentence code is provable in the theory.

results.title: Consistent formal theory
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A formal theory $T$ is consistent when $T$ does not prove the false sentence.

results.title: Soundness for halting sentences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A formal theory $T$ is sound for halting sentences when, for every $n$ and every Busy Beaver machine $M$ with $n$ states, if $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$ then $M$ halts on the blank tape, and if $T$ proves the non-halting sentence of $M$ then $M$ does not halt on the blank tape.

results.title: Theories deciding halting at a state count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A formal theory $T$ decides halting for $n$-state machines when, for every $n$-state machine $M$, $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$ or $T$ proves the non-halting sentence of $M$.

results.title: First undecidable number of states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a formal theory $T$, the first undecidable number of states is the least $n$ such that $T$ does not decide halting for all $n$-state machines, that is, there is an $n$-state machine $M$ for which $T$ proves neither the halting sentence nor the non-halting sentence of $M$. It is $0$ when there is no such $n$.

results.title: Decidability through five states and the first undecidable size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a formal theory $T$ decides halting for $n$-state machines for every $n \le 5$, and fails to decide halting for $n$-state machines for some $n$, then the first undecidable size of $T$ is at least $6$.

results.title: A consistency-search machine blocks decidability at its size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a formal theory and $M$ a Busy Beaver machine with $n$ working states. Suppose that $M$ halts if and only if $T$ proves the false sentence, that $M$ halts whenever $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$, that $T$ is consistent, and that $T$ does not prove the non-halting sentence of $M$. Then $T$ does not decide halting for all machines with $n$ working states.

results.title: Decidability of halting passes to fewer states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a formal theory such that, for every $m$ and every Busy Beaver machine $M$ with $m$ working states, if $T$ proves the halting sentence of the embedding of $M$ into $m + 1$ states then $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$, and if $T$ proves the non-halting sentence of the embedding of $M$ into $m + 1$ states then $T$ proves the non-halting sentence of $M$. Then for every $n$, if $T$ decides halting for…

results.title: Proof-checker presentation of a ZFC-like theory
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A ZFC-like presentation consists of a formal theory $T$, given by a provability predicate on sentence codes in $\mathbb{N}$, together with a Boolean proof checker $\mathrm{check}(p, s)$ on pairs of natural numbers, such that the following hold. A sentence code $s$ is provable in $T$ if and only if $\mathrm{check}(p, s)$ is true for some $p \in \mathbb{N}$. $T$ is sound for halting: for every machine $M$, if $T$…

results.title: ZFC-like theories decide halting through five states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every ZFC-like presentation $Z$ and every $n \le 5$, the theory presented by $Z$ decides halting for $n$-state machines: for every $n$-state machine it proves the machine's halting sentence or its non-halting sentence.

results.title: Three-state Busy Beaver shift value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Rado's shift function $S$ satisfies $S(3) = 21$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $3$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest halting time is $21$.

results.title: Three-state Busy Beaver score value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Rado's score function $\Sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma(3) = 6$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $3$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest number of ones left on the tape at the halting time is $6$.

results.title: Four-state Busy Beaver shift value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Rado's shift function $S$ satisfies $S(4) = 107$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $4$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest halting time is $107$.

results.title: Four-state Busy Beaver score value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Rado's score function $\Sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma(4) = 13$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $4$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest number of ones left on the tape at the halting time is $13$.

results.title: Five-state Busy Beaver shift value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Rado's shift function $S$ satisfies $S(5) = 47176870$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $5$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest halting time is $47176870$.

results.title: Five-state Busy Beaver score value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Rado's score function $\Sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma(5) = 4098$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $5$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest number of ones left on the tape at the halting time is $4098$.

results.title: Subtraction by addition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words and let $\bar y$ be the bitwise complement of $y$. Adding $x$ and $\bar y$ with carry in $1$ gives the $n$-bit result $x - y$ (the difference modulo $2^n$), and the carry out is $1$ exactly when there is no unsigned borrow, that is, when $y \le x$ as unsigned integers.

results.title: The ripple-carry adder subtracts
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words and let $\bar y$ be the bitwise complement of $y$. Evaluate the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $\bar y$ and carry in $1$. Then for every $i < n$, output $i$ is bit $i$ (counting from the least significant bit $0$) of $x - y$ modulo $2^n$.

results.title: Carry out of ripple-carry subtraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words and let $\bar y$ be the bitwise complement of $y$. Evaluate the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $\bar y$ and carry in $1$. Its carry out (output $n$) is $1$ exactly when there is no unsigned borrow in $x - y$, that is, when $y \le x$ as unsigned integers.

results.title: The carry-lookahead adder subtracts
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words, let $\bar y$ be the bitwise complement of $y$, and let $K$ satisfy $n \le 2^K$. Evaluate the $n$-bit carry-lookahead adder with $K$ levels, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $\bar y$ and carry in $1$. Then for every $i < n$, output $i$ is bit $i$ (counting from the least significant bit $0$) of $x - y$ modulo $2^n$.

results.title: Signed overflow is the XOR of the last two carries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words. The two's complement addition $x + y$ overflows (the sum of the two's complement values of $x$ and $y$ is at least $2^{n-1}$ or less than $-2^{n-1}$) exactly when the carry into the sign bit $n - 1$ differs from the carry out of it, both carries taken when adding $x$ and $y$ with carry in $0$.

results.title: The overflow adder
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The $n$-bit overflow adder is the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder with one extra XOR gate. It has the same $2n + 1$ inputs (the bits of the two summands, then the carry in) and $5n + 1$ gates: the $5n$ gates of the ripple-carry adder, followed by an XOR of the carry into bit $n - 1$ and the carry into bit $n$ (the carry out). Here the carry into bit $0$ is the carry in, and for $n = 0$ the index $n - 1$ is read as $0$.…

results.title: The overflow adder extends the ripple-carry adder
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words and let $c$ be a carry-in bit. Evaluate the $n$-bit overflow adder and the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $y$ and $c$. Then for every $o < n + 1$, output $o$ of the overflow adder equals output $o$ of the ripple-carry adder: the first $n + 1$ outputs (the $n$ sum bits and the carry out) agree.

results.title: The overflow flag
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words. Evaluate the $n$-bit overflow adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $y$ and carry in $0$. Its last output (output $n + 1$) is $1$ exactly when the two's complement addition $x + y$ overflows, that is, when the sum of the two's complement values of $x$ and $y$ is at least $2^{n-1}$ or less than $-2^{n-1}$.

results.title: Sum bits of the overflow adder
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words. Evaluate the $n$-bit overflow adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $y$ and carry in $0$. Then for every $i < n$, output $i$ is bit $i$ (counting from the least significant bit $0$) of $x + y$ modulo $2^n$.

results.title: Size of the overflow adder
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The $n$-bit overflow adder has $5n + 1$ gates.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $x_i$ be points in a real inner product space and $s$ a finite set of indices. The centroid of the points indexed by $s$ is $\frac{1}{|s|} \sum_{i \in s} x_i$; when $s$ is empty it is the zero vector.

results.title: Nearest-center assignment
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given points $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$) in a normed additive commutative group $E$ and centers $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1} \in E$, an assignment $a : \iota \to \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ assigns every point to a nearest center when $\|x_i - c_{a(i)}\| \le \|x_i - c_j\|$ for every index $i \in \iota$ and every $j < k$.

results.title: Nearest-center assignments exist
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any points $x_i$ in a normed additive commutative group and any centers $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1}$ with $k \ge 1$, there is an assignment that sends every point to a nearest center.

results.title: The k-means cost
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For points $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite type) in a normed additive commutative group, an assignment $a$ of each point $i$ to a cluster $a(i) \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ and centers $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1}$, the $k$-means cost is $\sum_{i \in \iota} \lVert x_i - c_{a(i)} \rVert^2$, the sum of the squared distances from the points to their assigned centers.

results.title: The cost as a sum over clusters
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For points $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite type) in a normed additive commutative group, an assignment $a$ of each point $i$ to a cluster $a(i) \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ and centers $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1}$, the $k$-means cost equals $\sum_{j} \sum_{i : a(i) = j} \lVert x_i - c_j \rVert^2$: for each cluster $j$, add up the squared distances from the points assigned to $j$ to its center $c_j$.

results.title: The centroid update step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite type) be points in a real inner product space and let $a$ assign each point $i$ to a cluster $a(i) \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$. The updated centers send each cluster $j$ to the centroid of the points $x_i$ with $a(i) = j$. A cluster with no points gets the center $0$, which does not affect the $k$-means cost of $a$.

results.title: The update step never increases the cost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a fixed assignment, the centroids are the best centers.

results.title: The assignment step never increases the cost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For fixed centers, nearest-center assignment is optimal.

results.title: One round of Lloyd's algorithm never increases the cost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Recompute the centers, then reassign every point to a nearest new center.

results.title: The cost never increases along a run of Lloyd's algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The cost never increases along a run of Lloyd's algorithm.

results.title: Runs of Lloyd's algorithm exist
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite type) be points in a real inner product space and let $k \ge 1$. Every starting assignment $a_0$ of the points to clusters $0, \dots, k-1$ and every choice of starting centers $c_0$ extend to a run of Lloyd's algorithm: there are assignments $a_t$ and centers $c_t$ for $t \in \mathbb{N}$, equal to $a_0$ and $c_0$ at $t = 0$, that form a run.
